enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION C: PRESCRIBED TEXTS (20 marks)**

Answer ONE question only.

**1.** *Read the following extract from John Ngong Kum Ngong's* Walls of Agony *and answer the questions that follow.*

**"Walls of Agony"**

They upset ingenious minds
And fill porous hearts with fear,
Colossal walls of agony
Seeking to secrete their masters
Inside polythene bags of myth,  **[5]**
Hurling insults at me and my tribe.

We are like the farmer
Who harvested cash crops
But crawled to the market square,
Patched and pallid like tatters  **[10]**
To beg and look for refuge.
We who yesterday without walls
Wove our way through impenetrable hearts,
Resolved to make Cameroon a paradise.

Flamboyant tricksters talk of love  **[15]**
Springing from their hearts like fountains
But we feel the pinch of their contempt
Perched on the warped walls of their minds,
Searching where to *raise new walls of bondage.*
They seek to *mount gigantic breweries*  **[20]**
Where we often planted cassava.
They seek to defame our defiant walls
*To seduce us into sedition*
And *bury our resistance before birth.*
They nauseate filthy minds  **[25]**
And fill feeling hearts with rage
These gargantuan walls of misery
Ready to cover their masters
From the punches of dissatisfied hearts,
Raining curses at me and my clan.  **[30]**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**a.** Give the meaning in context of the following expressions:

(i) '...*to raise new walls of bondage*' (line 19) (1 mark)

(ii) '...*mount gigantic breweries*' (line 20) (1 mark)

(iii) '... *seduce us into sedition*' (line 23) (1 mark)

(iv) '... *bury our resistance before birth*' (line 24) (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answers** (one clear meaning in context for each expression; 1 mark each)

| Expression | Meaning in context |
|---|---|
| (i) "to raise new walls of bondage" (line 19) | To build fresh barriers of slavery, that is, to invent new systems of oppression and control that keep ordinary people captive and powerless. The "tricksters" are looking for new ways to enslave the people. |
| (ii) "mount gigantic breweries" (line 20) | To set up huge beer-making factories on the very land where the villagers used to grow their food (cassava). The expression shows how the oppressors take over the people's land and livelihood for their own profit. |
| (iii) "seduce us into sedition" (line 23) | To tempt or trick us, with charming words and false promises, into rebelling or acting against authority, so that we can be accused and punished. |
| (iv) "bury our resistance before birth" (line 24) | To crush and destroy our opposition at its very beginning, before it has had time to take shape or grow. |

**Tip.** "In context" means that the meaning must fit the poem: it is not enough to give a dictionary meaning of "sedition" or "brewery"; say what the expression shows about the oppressors and the people.

**Common mistakes**

1. Explaining the words one by one (for example "brewery = a place where beer is made") without saying what the phrase means in the poem.
2. Taking "walls" and "breweries" literally instead of seeing the figurative meaning (oppression, exploitation of the land).
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: **b.** Briefly say what you consider to be the message in the poem. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer**

The poem denounces deceitful and selfish leaders who oppress ordinary people. Although they speak of love, they build "walls of agony": they hide behind myths, insult the people, take the land on which villagers grow their food and look for new ways to enslave them, all to protect their own masters. The poet also shows that the people are not helpless. They work hard, they are resolved "to make Cameroon a paradise" and they remain "defiant". The message is therefore a warning against political deceit and exploitation, and an encouragement to the people to stay united, vigilant and resistant.

**What earns the marks (3 marks)**

| Point | Mark |
|---|---|
| The oppression and deceit of the leaders ("flamboyant tricksters", "walls of agony", "myth") | 1 |
| The exploitation and humiliation of the people (the farmer in rags, breweries on cassava land, insults and curses) | 1 |
| The people's resilience and hope, and the call to resist and to build a better country | 1 |

**Common mistakes**

1. Paraphrasing the poem stanza by stanza instead of stating the message in a few sentences.
2. Giving only the negative side (oppression) and ignoring the defiance and resolve of "we".

*Note: this is a reading based on the printed text of the poem; the Board's official answer is not available.*
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown: **c.** Identify and comment on the use of any two figures of speech from the poem. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model answer (two figures, 2 marks each)**

**1. Metaphor: "polythene bags of myth" (line 5).** The leaders' lies and false stories are compared to polythene bags in which they hide their masters. The image is concrete and everyday: polythene is cheap, flimsy and thrown away, so the poet suggests that the myths are artificial and fragile, yet they are used to cover and protect the real masters from the people's anger. The same device appears in "walls of agony" (line 3), where suffering becomes a wall that imprisons the people.

**2. Simile: "We are like the farmer / Who harvested cash crops / But crawled to the market square, / Patched and pallid like tatters" (lines 7 to 10).** The people are compared to a farmer who produces wealth (cash crops) but is himself reduced to rags and begging. The comparison shows the injustice of exploitation: the one who works the land does not enjoy its fruits. "Pallid" and "tatters" give a clear picture of weakness and poverty, and they make the reader feel pity and anger.

**Other acceptable figures**

| Figure | Example | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Simile | "Springing from their hearts like fountains" (line 16) | Their loving words flow easily and falsely, like water, which exposes their hypocrisy |
| Hyperbole | "Colossal walls", "gigantic breweries", "gargantuan walls of misery" | The size of the oppression and of the oppressors' greed is made enormous |
| Alliteration | "Flamboyant tricksters" (line 15), "feel the pinch" (line 17), "fill feeling hearts" (line 26) | The repeated sounds make the lines forceful and emphasise the accusation |
| Personification | "the punches of dissatisfied hearts" (line 29) | The hearts of the angry people are shown as fighters who strike back |
| Irony | "talk of love ... the pinch of their contempt" (lines 15 to 17) | Their words say one thing and their behaviour the opposite |

**Common mistakes**

1. Naming a figure without quoting it, or quoting without commenting on its effect (each figure earns its marks only with identification and comment).
2. Mixing up metaphor and simile: a simile uses "like" or "as"; a metaphor does not.
themes: A Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown:
**d.** (i) Change the following statements into the past perfect tense:

- '*They upset ingenious minds*' (line 1) (1 mark)
- '*Flamboyant tricksters talk of love*' (line 15) (1 mark)

(ii) Pick out any three adjectives from the last nine lines of the last stanza of the poem and transform them into adverbs. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Past perfect (had + past participle)**

- "They upset ingenious minds" becomes **"They had upset ingenious minds."** (upset is the same in the past participle)
- "Flamboyant tricksters talk of love" becomes **"Flamboyant tricksters had talked of love."**

**(ii) Adjectives changed into adverbs (the last nine lines of the poem are lines 22 to 30)**

| Adjective | Line | Adverb | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| defiant | 22 ("our defiant walls") | **defiantly** | add -ly |
| filthy | 25 ("filthy minds") | **filthily** | final -y becomes -i, then add -ly |
| feeling | 26 ("feeling hearts") | **feelingly** | add -ly |

Other possible choices: "gargantuan" (line 27) gives "gargantuanly" and "dissatisfied" (line 29) gives "dissatisfiedly"; both adverbs are correct in form but rare, so the three above are the safest.

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing "had upset" as "had upsetted", or using the simple past ("talked") instead of the past perfect.
2. Spelling "filthy" as "filthyly": a final -y after a consonant becomes -i before -ly.
3. Choosing words that are not adjectives (for example "gargantuan" is fine, but "walls" or "hearts" are nouns).

questions.enonce_markdown: **e.** How is the message treated in this poem reflected in any other two prescribed texts? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Corrigé de méthode (the prescribed texts themselves are not available, so no detail of any other work is given here)**

**Step 1 - Fix the message.** State it in one sentence, as established in question (b): leaders who deceive and exploit ordinary people, and the people's resilience and resistance.

**Step 2 - Choose two other prescribed texts** that you know well (any genre: novel, play or poem) and that treat a similar idea, for example abuse of power, deceit, exploitation, injustice or resistance.

**Step 3 - For each text, write one short paragraph** (about 2 marks per text):

1. Name the text and its author, and say which part of the message it reflects.
2. Give ONE precise example (a character, an event or a quotation) that shows the idea at work.
3. Say how the writer treats it (tone, point of view, device) and, if possible, one similarity or difference with the poem: the poem uses images such as "walls" and "myth", whereas a novel or play uses characters and events.

**Sentence frame.** "The message of oppression and resistance in 'Walls of Agony' is also found in [title] by [author]. For example, [character/event] shows [idea]. Like the poet, the writer [treatment]."

**What earns the marks (4 marks):** for each of the two texts, 1 mark for a relevant link with the message and 1 mark for an accurate, specific example.

**Common mistakes**

1. Summarising the whole plot of the other texts instead of linking one precise example to the message.
2. Choosing a text whose theme has no real link with the poem, or repeating the same example for both texts.
3. Using the poem again instead of "other" texts: the question asks for TWO OTHER prescribed texts.
